name: MiraJet

lead: MiraJet is a clinic device from JSK Biomed that uses laser energy to create a high-pressure microjet that delivers substances such as hyaluronic acid, botulinum toxin, vitamins or platelet-rich plasma into the dermis without a needle.

The appearance goal is smoother, more hydrated, firmer-looking skin and improved scars, with supporters pointing to less pain than needle injections. Published studies are small split-face and case series, and the manufacturer-linked descriptions are the main source of mechanism claims.

paras: A clinician loads the product into the handpiece and fires many tiny shots across the treatment area, reaching about 2 mm depth per the manufacturer description. Sessions are repeated according to the product used, and downtime is described as short.

Tiny pinpoint bleeding or petechiae is the main reported effect. Needle-free injectors in general raise cross-contamination concerns when nozzles are reused, so single-use tips are important. The device is used in clinics, so a clinician decides suitability.

angle.text: A clinic uses MiraJet in place of a needle to place skin boosters or other products in the dermis for smoother, more hydrated skin and softer scars. Supporters emphasise reduced pain compared with needles.

lead: MiraJet is a laser-driven, needle-free microjet system from JSK Biomed that converts light energy into pressure to drive a drug through the skin [1]. Needle-free jet injectors push a narrow high-pressure stream of liquid through the skin without a needle [2].

In aesthetics it is used to deliver hyaluronic acid, botulinum toxins, vitamins and platelet-rich plasma to roughly 2 mm depth in the dermis, in doses of 0.1 to 0.3 mL per shot, for concerns such as skin rejuvenation, pigmentation, acne scars, stretch marks and lifting [1].

A 2021 review of needle-free injectors in dermatology concluded that they have potential in skin remodelling and rejuvenation using various aesthetic materials [3]. Two 2024 studies reported using the microjet with poly-D,L-lactic acid for atrophic scars and rosacea [4][5].
infobox: Hyaluronic acid, botulinum toxin, vitamins, PRP, PDLLA

paras: The manufacturer-linked description says light energy is turned into pressure so the drug penetrates the skin; the jet reaches about 2 mm, delivers 0.1 to 0.3 mL per shot and fires up to 2,400 microshots per minute. The proposed mechanism also includes microholes stimulating fibroblasts and collagen regeneration [1]. Jet injectors in general use a spring, gas or laser-driven pressure to drive a thin stream of liquid through the skin [2].

A dermatologist's account lists hyaluronic acid, botulinum toxin, vitamins and platelet-rich plasma as products delivered with the device, for melasma, pigmentation, acne and burn scars, stretch marks and volumizing [1]. She also reports using poly-D,L-lactic acid for pitted acne scars [1].

Fine petechiae or pinpoint bleeding with little downtime are described [1]. Jet injectors with reusable nozzles have a documented history of cross-contamination, including a hepatitis B outbreak linked to a 1984-85 weight-loss clinic, which is why single-use components matter [2].

Published work on microjet delivery includes a 2024 study of poly-D,L-lactic acid for atrophic scars in Asian patients [4] and a 2024 study for rosacea in Asian patients [5]. A 2021 literature review summarised dermatology applications of needle-free injectors generally [3]. Studies are small, and a separate expert interview reports clinic experience rather than controlled data [1].
